old: At its core sits a very old idea: the other one, not yourself.
It comes from a French legal phrase about 'the good, the right of the other.'
A philosopher named Comte coined it in 1830 — and it shares a root with the English word 'alter.'
clues: This quality of character was invented on purpose by a French philosopher, Auguste Comte, rather than evolving naturally like most words.
It means unselfish concern for others' welfare as a principle, broader than charity or generosity. Comte was apparently inspired by a French legal phrase about 'the good of the other.'
Its opposite is egoism, and an 'effective' movement devoted to doing the most good bears its name. It shares a Latin root meaning 'other' with the word alter.
